title: Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules
shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication M...
summary: On Linux, Unix and macOS, authentication is assembled from pluggable authentication modules, a modular set of configuration files, shared libraries and helper binaries that services call when a user signs in. A service names its configuration, that configuration lists modules in order, and the modules consult files such as the password and shadow files to verify the supplied secret. An adversary who can write to these paths can replace or patch a module so that it accepts a value of their choosing, allowing sign-in without any valid password. The same position supports credential theft, because pluggable authentication modules do not store passwords and therefore receive them in plain text, so injected code inside a module can log every password the host sees, whether typed at a console or sent over the network to a service. Artefacts include changed library hashes and modification times, new or edited configuration files under the module configuration directory, and unexpected network or file activity from a process in the authentication stack. Distributions legitimately update these libraries, so compare against package manager records and integrity baselines first.

beginner.definition: On Linux and similar systems, sign-in checks are built from small parts called pluggable authentication modules. These modules are listed in configuration files. This technique means an attacker changes one of those parts, either to steal passwords or to let themselves in.
beginner.whyItMatters: The modules see passwords in plain text, because they must compare them with the stored values. A single changed module can collect passwords from every service on the host. It can also add a hidden way to sign in that keeps working after a password reset. Without file monitoring, such a change can stay on a busy server for years.
howItWorks: Each service, such as sign-in, secure shell, or sudo, names a configuration file for its checks.
That configuration lists modules, which are shared libraries loaded in a set order.
The modules read the account files and compare the supplied secret with the stored value.
An attacker replaces or patches a module so that it also accepts one chosen value.
They may also add code that writes every plaintext password to a hidden file.
Because the modules already run during sign-in, the extra work is very easy to miss.
beginner.example: Think of a large office where each door has its own checker holding a printed checklist. Every checker follows the same rules, taken from a shared manual in the lobby. Somebody swaps one page of that manual, so the east door now opens for a particular word. Staff still pass through normally, and the checklists look unchanged at a glance. The same person also stands quietly at the door and writes down every password people say out loud.
takeaways: Pluggable authentication modules handle plaintext passwords, so their files must be protected.
Use file integrity monitoring on module libraries and their configuration files.
A module or configuration file that no package owns is a strong sign of tampering.

objectives: Describe the role of pluggable authentication modules in Unix-style authentication.
Explain how a modified module can bypass checks or capture credentials.
Locate the configuration files and libraries involved in this authentication system.
Explain how package records and file integrity tools help identify tampering.
Recommend controls that limit who can write to authentication components.
